mcqs.question: Which pairing correctly matches a risk introduced by bare retries with its fix?
options: Retry storms are fixed by adding more retry attempts
Duplicate effects are fixed by retrying faster
Masked failures are fixed by capping the retry count and surfacing the failure once the cap is reached, instead of retrying forever
Duplicate effects are fixed by exponential backoff alone
mcqs.explanation: Masked failures happen when retries hide a persistent problem indefinitely; capping attempts and surfacing the failure once the cap is hit is what exposes it. More attempts worsens retry storms rather than fixing them, and duplicate effects need idempotency, not speed or backoff timing.

mcqs.question: Why does exponential backoff alone, without jitter, fail to fully solve the retry-storm problem?
options: Every client that failed at the same moment still retries at the same later moment, just delayed, keeping their retries synchronized
Backoff without jitter causes requests to never be retried at all
Backoff makes each individual request take longer to process on the server
Backoff without jitter is not supported by any HTTP client library
mcqs.explanation: Backoff alone just shifts the synchronized retry to a later, still-synchronized point in time — clients that failed together still retry together. Jitter is what breaks the synchronization by randomizing each client's wait. It doesn't prevent retries entirely, doesn't slow server-side processing, and is a client-side pattern any HTTP library can implement.

mcqs.question: When should you fail fast instead of retrying a failed request?
options: Only when the request is a GET
Never — every failure should be retried at least once
When the failure is clearly non-transient (like a 400 for malformed input) or when downstream is showing sustained trouble, often signaled by a tripped circuit breaker
mcqs.explanation: Failing fast makes sense when a retry can't help — a malformed request will fail identically every time — or when a circuit breaker has already detected sustained downstream trouble and adding more retry load would only make it worse. It isn't limited to GET requests, isn't never appropriate, and has nothing to do with time of day.

mcqs.question: What's the specific danger of retrying a failed request indefinitely with no cap?
options: It becomes illegal under most API terms of service
It guarantees the request will eventually succeed
Unbounded in-flight retries can exhaust the client's own resources and keep piling load onto a downstream service, actively preventing it from recovering
It causes the request to be processed twice as fast
mcqs.explanation: Uncapped retries accumulate as unbounded in-flight work on the client and unbounded additional load on a struggling downstream service, which can prevent recovery rather than wait it out. It doesn't guarantee eventual success, isn't a terms-of-service issue, and doesn't speed up processing.
